description: CADS-dataset is a large-scale collection of 22,022 CT volumes with voxel-level annotations covering 167 anatomical structures for whole-body CT segmentation. The dataset aggregates CT scans from over 40 diverse sources spanning more than 100 imaging facilities across 16 countries, collected between 2007 and 2024. It includes both publicly sourced data and two newly contributed collections (484 head CTs and 586 triphasic contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scans), covering a wide spectrum of clinical variability including healthy subjects and various pathological conditions.
license: other (composite dataset; users must comply with individual licenses of each source dataset — see dataset documentation and original publications for details)
name: CADS-dataset
rai:annotatorDemographics: Three in-house medical research assistants and a radiation oncologist (Jan C. Peeken) contributed manual annotations for the VISCERAL Gold Corpus dataset. Expert review of clinical segmentations was conducted by an experienced radiation oncologist with 5.5 years in practice. Reference annotation masks for the University Hospital Zurich cohort were generated using MIM software and validated by medical doctors, or directly contoured by radiation oncologists following standard clinical protocols.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Annotation quality was assessed through: (1) automated shape-based outlier detection using neural implicit functions — pseudo-labels with 90th-percentile Hausdorff distance above threshold were excluded; (2) statistical flavor selection using Dice Similarity Coefficient as primary metric and HD95 as secondary metric, with Shapiro-Wilk normality tests, Levene's variance equality tests, and ANOVA/Welch's ANOVA/Kruskal-Wallis tests with post-hoc comparisons (Tukey's HSD or Dunn's test, p<0.05); (3) manual expert review of 65 test images from TotalSegmentator dataset by in-house medical professionals, classifying each annotation as reliable or unreliable with documented error descriptions; (4) expert radiation oncologist review of clinical segmentations via systematic slice-by-slice assessment.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: In-house annotation by medical research assistants and radiation oncologist; MIM software used for reference annotation masks in the University Hospital Zurich evaluation cohort
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: A multi-stage annotation pipeline was used: (1) Pseudo-labeling: 167 target structures were organized into nine anatomical groups; specialized nnU-Net models were trained on high-quality annotations from established datasets and used to generate pseudo-labels across all 22,022 CT scans. (2) Shape-informed quality control: automated outlier detection using neural implicit functions trained on ground-truth segmentations; pseudo-labels with high 90th-percentile Hausdorff distance were excluded (lowest-scoring 10% removed). (3) Multi-strategy label optimization: three complementary model "flavors" were trained (GT-flavor on original ground truth, Pseudo-flavor on all pseudo-labeled data, Shape-flavor on quality-filtered pseudo-labels); statistical ranking (Dice + HD95, using ANOVA/Welch's ANOVA/Kruskal-Wallis with post-hoc tests) selected the best-performing flavor per structure. (4) Final label assembly: best-flavor pseudo-labels were merged with original GT annotations taking highest priority. Additional manual annotations were contributed by three in-house medical research assistants and a radiation oncologist for the VISCERAL Gold Corpus dataset.
rai:dataBiases: The paper acknowledges several bias-related considerations: (1) Only 21% of publicly available CT scans contain any annotations, with annotations typically confined to a single organ system, creating annotation imbalance. (2) The shape-based quality control exclusion strategy may eliminate cases involving pathological conditions with atypical anatomical variations, potentially limiting the model's ability to learn clinically important edge scenarios. (3) Class imbalance exists in the dataset — structures like uppermost cervical vertebrae (C1-C5) appear less frequently across the 22,022 volumes. (4) Facial features are intentionally anonymized due to privacy considerations, limiting applications requiring detailed facial analysis. (5) The data-centric approach using pseudo-labeling and multi-source integration was specifically designed to mitigate variance-driven errors, boundary ambiguity, protocol heterogeneity, and inter-annotator inconsistency through aggregation across diverse instances.
rai:dataCollection: The CADS-dataset aggregates CT scans from three main source categories: (1) large-scale public archives including TotalSegmentator (1,203 annotated volumes), NLST (7,172 scans), CT-RATE (3,134 scans), and AbdomenCT-1K (1,062 scans); (2) specialized annotation collections from medical imaging challenges (Grand Challenge, MICCAI) and focused research studies (Han-Seg, SAROS, TCIA oncology studies); and (3) newly contributed images comprising 484 anonymized head CTs from Istanbul Medipol University and 586 triphasic contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scans from TUM Klinikum Rechts der Isar. The collection spans more than 100 imaging facilities across 16 countries. Selection criteria focused on CT scans covering key anatomical regions throughout the body including brain, head-and-neck, thorax, abdomen, pelvis, and femur.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consists of 22,022 volumetric CT scans in original image formats from 40 diverse sources. Of these, 4,695 (approximately 21%) contain partial manual or hybrid annotations from public sources, while approximately 79% lack any annotations. Sources include public archives (TCIA, Grand Challenge, MICCAI challenges), research collections, and newly acquired hospital CT scans. The dataset covers varying imaging protocols (contrast-enhanced and non-contrast acquisitions) and multiple anatomical fields of view (whole-body, head-and-neck, chest, abdomen, pelvis, spine).
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, Physical data collection
rai:dataImputationProtocol: For the SAROS dataset which provides sparse slice-based 2D annotations (labels available only on selected slices), interpolation between annotated slices was performed to create dense 3D per-slice annotations required for volumetric training.
rai:dataLimitations: The paper identifies several limitations: (1) The shape-based quality control exclusion strategy may eliminate pathological cases with atypical anatomical variations, limiting learning of clinically important edge scenarios. (2) Coverage is limited to head to knees; hands, feet, and finer vascular substructures are not included. (3) Several structures require refinement: brain mask is broadly defined including all CNS components within skull; optic chiasm tends to be under-segmented; heart segmentation omits superior portions; rectum appears shorter than anatomical extent; trachea is limited to air content without surrounding cartilage wall; vena cava delineation is imprecise. (4) Facial features are intentionally anonymized, limiting detailed facial analysis applications. (5) Some structures have limited training data (e.g., buccal mucosa appears in fewer than 1,000 scans with only 30 ground-truth annotations). (6) Very small organs (volumes below 0.5 mL) are challenging due to standard CT resolution limits and partial volume effects.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Post-collection manipulations include: (1) oversampling with inverse-probability class weights to address class imbalance (e.g., less frequent C1-C5 vertebrae receive higher sampling weights); (2) targeted subset creation for specialized anatomical regions (e.g., images with predicted brain voxel count >2,000 for brain group; images with at least 24 target structures for head-and-neck group); (3) rib segmentation refinement: connected components analysis with majority voting for consistent rib labeling, and costovertebral joint retrieval using vesselFM with morphological opening and size filtering (100–1,500 voxels); (4) head pseudo-label postprocessing: exclusion of scans with brain voxel count <2,000, and bounding-box cropping around brain centroid (±[100,100,133] voxels for brain structures; ±[100,100,200] voxels for head-and-neck structures).
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: A three-step standardization pipeline was applied: (1) reorientation of all images to standard RAS (Right-Anterior-Superior) convention; (2) resampling to uniform 1.5 mm isotropic resolution to balance segmentation accuracy with computational efficiency; (3) simplification of original affine transformation matrices by removing rotation and translation components, preserving only scaling and shear. For patient privacy in newly acquired hospital head CT scans, a Gaussian filter (σ=5 voxels at 1.5 mm spacing) was applied to facial regions to obscure identity while preserving structural integrity.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to advance robust AI solutions in radiology and make comprehensive anatomical analysis accessible to clinicians and researchers. Clinical applications include: streamlining radiation therapy treatment planning through rapid organ delineation; enabling automated organ volume quantification and detection of subtle anatomical changes in diagnostic radiology; facilitating large-scale population studies across diverse populations and conditions. The dataset's geographic diversity spanning 16 countries and over 100 medical centers is designed to capture varied clinical practices and patient populations, supporting development of generalizable AI tools. The open-source release of dataset, models, and clinical tools (3D Slicer plugin) aims to reduce accessibility barriers for healthcare practitioners without technical expertise.
rai:dataUseCases: Intended use cases include: (1) training and evaluation of whole-body CT segmentation models; (2) radiation therapy treatment planning through organ-at-risk delineation; (3) automated organ volume quantification and abnormality detection in diagnostic radiology; (4) anatomical landmark detection for automated measurements; (5) cross-modality registration for CT-MRI fusion and PET-CT alignment; (6) anatomy-guided image reconstruction for radiation dose reduction; (7) longitudinal organ tracking and personalized anatomical modeling; (8) large-scale population studies; (9) body composition analysis through tissue quantification; (10) localization of metastases; (11) region-specific abnormality detection for triage and mortality risk assessment.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: nnU-Net framework (version 2.5.1) used for training specialized segmentation models and generating pseudo-labels; neural implicit functions (auto-decoder based on implicit neural representations) used for shape-based quality control; vesselFM (a foundation model for 3D blood vessel segmentation) used for rib costovertebral joint retrieval; ANTs (Advanced Normalization Tools) non-rigid transformation used for brain structure annotation via registration with SimNIBS MRI atlas; interpolation between annotated slices used for SAROS dataset 3D annotation generation.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: All newly acquired hospital CT scans are anonymized. For the 484 head CT scans from Istanbul Medipol University, a Gaussian filter (σ=5 voxels at 1.5 mm spacing) was applied to facial regions to obscure patient identity. The 586 triphasic contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scans from TUM Klinikum Rechts der Isar are described as anonymized. Ethics approvals were obtained from the Clinical Research Ethics Committee at Istanbul Medipol University and the Ethics Committee of the Technical University of Munich (TUM).

null_reasons.rai:annotationsPerItem: The paper does not specify a fixed number of independent annotations per item; annotations vary by source dataset and structure, with some from single annotators and others from automated pipelines.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The paper does not explicitly discuss missing data handling such as cloud filtering or incomplete records; the 79% unannotated scans are addressed through pseudo-labeling rather than imputation.
null_reasons.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: No versioning, update cadence, or maintenance plan is described in the paper.
